paragraphs: A further difficulty emerged when the planners discussed how the new information should appear on a public sign. If every possible circumstance were included, the sign would become too crowded to guide anyone; if all the qualifications disappeared, the old mistake would return in a more attractive design. They therefore tested a display which asked walkers first to select a time of travel and then to consider whether they needed a seat. The temperatures remained visible, but the order of the questions prevented the lowest number from silently becoming a recommendation for everyone who happened to read it.

Not until the trial had included people whose walking pace differed substantially did the team notice another limitation. A bench shown on the sign could be occupied when it was needed, leaving a person who could not stand for long with no practical alternative. The revised display consequently identified places where several seats were available and made clear that availability was not guaranteed. This was a less impressive promise than the original proposal, yet a more defensible one: the town could improve the information on which a choice depended without pretending to control every circumstance in which that choice would be made.

When a school group visited, a pupil asked whether the grey areas could simply be filled with drawings of the activities that probably occurred there. The suggestion was attractive because it would make the harbour look alive, but the curator distinguished an illustration used to raise a question from an image offered as a record. A drawing accompanied by an explanation of its evidential basis might serve the former purpose. Placed among the blue marks without such a distinction, however, it would allow a plausible reconstruction to borrow the authority of the documents from which the rest of the map had been made.

The archive subsequently invited visitors to compare a shipping diary with the tax records. The diary mentioned temporary unloading places but did not locate them precisely, so the sources could not be combined into a single map without further judgement.

Rather than colouring an entire uncertain stretch blue, the curator displayed the diary passage beside the map and explained the unresolved relationship. What made this addition informative was not that it removed uncertainty, but that it changed the question visitors could reasonably ask. They could now investigate how two kinds of record differed in what they preserved, instead of choosing between complete confidence in the map and complete rejection of it.

To discover whether the new exercise taught more than familiarity with its recordings, the instructors prepared a second set of cases. In one, a sound that had previously indicated a fault occurred while the machine was operating under a different load. Trainees who merely remembered the earlier answer were likely to stop at the sound, whereas those who compared the surrounding conditions asked for further information. Neither hesitation nor immediate certainty was treated as proof of competence on its own. The instructors examined whether the request for information concerned something that could actually change the diagnosis, rather than rewarding every request simply for sounding cautious.

Having reviewed the trainees' explanations, the technician revised her own account of the demonstration. She could now distinguish a feature which she had ignored because it was irrelevant from one which she had failed to consider because it was usually absent. The distinction mattered especially when a machine was moved into an unfamiliar environment. It was not the length of an explanation that made it educational, but its ability to expose a decision to meaningful comparison. A manual could record some of these comparisons; it could not anticipate every situation in which a once reasonable habit might cease to be reliable.

A later review raised a different objection: readers who were already familiar with the local practice might find the explanation unnecessary. The team accepted the point, but rejected the assumption that a label must serve every visitor in exactly the same way. A short heading could provide immediate orientation, while an optional second layer explained the obligations carried by the term.

This arrangement was tested with readers whose knowledge of farming varied. Some skipped the longer note and still identified the object correctly; others used it to revise an earlier impression that the owner was concerned only with lost income. The difference was useful only if the team kept the exhibition's purpose in view.

The editors also asked whether their explanation had turned a living practice into a fixed definition. Members of the community disagreed about how the obligations should be fulfilled, even though they recognized the term. A note which concealed that disagreement would preserve unfamiliar vocabulary while simplifying the idea it was meant to protect.

The final label therefore offered an example of the responsibility and acknowledged variation in its interpretation. Preserving a distinction did not require pretending that everyone understood it identically. Nor did acknowledging variation make the word meaningless: the disagreements themselves concerned a shared relationship which the proposed equivalent had omitted.

During a later workshop, visitors compared two replicas made from different materials. One reproduced fine surface details but was too delicate to grasp firmly; the other allowed the movement of a handle to be explored, although its texture was less faithful. Staff initially asked which copy was more accurate. The discussion became more productive when visitors asked what each copy was accurate about. A model designed to answer one question could mislead when used to answer another, even if every difference from the original had been carefully recorded. The record of a limitation did not by itself ensure that a visitor understood its significance.

The museum responded by placing a question beside each object rather than relying on a general warning that replicas were imperfect. Visitors were invited to explain which features supported their answers and which conclusions would require examining something else. Only when such explanations were considered did the staff discover that an apparently clear label had encouraged some visitors to treat smoothness as evidence of age.

Correcting that inference required a specific account of how the replica had been manufactured. The lesson was neither that copies inevitably deceive nor that access alone guarantees understanding. It was that useful access includes opportunities to examine the relationship between an experience and the claims made on its basis.
